title: Which statement about tokens is accurate?
scenario: You are budgeting an AI feature and want to reason correctly about limits and costs.
task: Which statement is the most accurate?

options.text: One token always equals one word.
options.feedback: A helpful myth — token counts depend on the tokenizer. “Cat” is often one token; “internationalization” is several; emojis can be multiple.

options.text: Token counts are approximate and depend on the model, the language and the content.
options.feedback: Yes — which is exactly why the ¾-word rule is only an estimate, and why dense text, code and other languages cost more.

options.text: Only your messages count; the model's replies are free.
options.feedback: Both input and output are counted — long answers add to the bill and fill the window too.

options.text: Accents and emojis never affect token counts.
options.feedback: Unusual characters are often split into multiple tokens — they can cost several times what plain letters do.

hints: The honest answer contains the word “depends”.
explanation: Tokens are slices, not words: the count depends on the model's tokenizer, the language and the content. Practical consequences: estimate with the ¾-word rule, expect code and emojis to cost more, and remember that both input and output count.
